name: Mexico City
tagline: Aztec ruins, mezcal bars and tacos al pastor beneath volcano skies
description:
Built on the drained bed of an Aztec lake and ringed by volcanoes, Mexico City is one of the planet's great metropolises and one of its most rewarding. Pyramids, colonial palaces and brutalist museums share the same streets, organ grinders crank out tunes beside Art Nouveau theaters, and the smell of charred corn and griddled tortillas follows you everywhere.

Start in the Centro Histórico, where the vast Zócalo is flanked by the cathedral and the excavated ruins of the Templo Mayor, then drift west to the marble Palacio de Bellas Artes. Spend a morning with the Aztec Sun Stone at the anthropology museum, an afternoon in Frida Kahlo's cobalt-blue house in Coyoacán and an evening in leafy Roma or Condesa, where Art Deco apartment blocks hide mezcal bars and some of the most exciting kitchens in the Americas.

Eating is the city's heartbeat. Street stands shave tacos al pastor off spinning spits, market counters ladle out steaming pozole, and tasting menus reinvent ancient ingredients like huitlacoche and chapulines. Add a boat party on the canals of Xochimilco, masked wrestlers at the arena and a sunrise balloon ride over Teotihuacan, and you'll see why a week never feels like enough.

safety.notes: Roma, Condesa, Polanco, Coyoacán and the Centro are fine to explore by day, but use Uber, DiDi or authorized sitio taxis rather than hailing cabs on the street at night. Pickpockets work the crowded Metro and markets, so keep your phone and wallet in front pockets.

tipping: Leave 10–15% at sit-down restaurants, where the server will bring the card terminal to the table and ask how much tip to add; also tip grocery baggers and gas-station attendants a few pesos.
gettingAround: The Metro is extensive and costs just a few pesos, but it gets crushingly packed at rush hour. Metrobús lines and Ecobici bikes are handy for hopping between the Centro, Roma and Condesa, and Uber or DiDi rides are cheap and safer than street taxis.
tips: The city sits at 2,240 meters, so take the first day slowly, drink plenty of water and go easy on the mezcal until you've acclimatized.
Don't drink the tap water; bottled water is everywhere, and the ice in restaurants and bars is made from purified water.
Most museums close on Mondays and many are free for Mexican residents on Sundays, which makes Sunday crowds intense; plan big sights for Tuesday to Friday.
Carry small bills and coins, because street stalls and markets often can't change a 500-peso note.
From June to September, heavy downpours arrive most afternoons like clockwork, so do outdoor sightseeing in the morning and keep an umbrella handy.
Reach Teotihuacan right at the 9 a.m. opening to beat the tour buses and the midday sun, as there is almost no shade on site.
etiquette: Say 'buenos días' or 'buenas tardes' when entering a shop, elevator or waiting room; skipping the greeting comes across as cold.
'Ahorita' can mean right now, later or never, so build some patience into your plans.
Lunch, or comida, is the main meal and runs from about 2 to 5 p.m.; dinner is lighter and later.
Locals rarely wear shorts in the city, so dress a notch smarter for nice restaurants and churches.

neighborhoods.name: Roma Norte
neighborhoods.blurb: Art Nouveau mansions and Art Deco apartment blocks line leafy streets packed with specialty coffee, galleries, mezcal bars and many of the city's most exciting restaurants.

neighborhoods.name: Condesa
neighborhoods.blurb: Built around two oval parks shaded by jacarandas, Condesa is made for strolling, dog-watching, long brunches and bar-hopping along the tree-lined loop of Avenida Ámsterdam.

neighborhoods.name: Coyoacán
neighborhoods.blurb: A colonial village swallowed by the city, with cobbled lanes, a lively plaza, churro stands, a bustling food market and Frida Kahlo's Blue House.

neighborhoods.name: Centro Histórico
neighborhoods.blurb: The historic heart, crammed with colonial palaces, Aztec ruins, old cantinas and street vendors, anchored by the Zócalo and the Palacio de Bellas Artes.

neighborhoods.name: Polanco
neighborhoods.blurb: The city's upscale enclave of designer boutiques, contemporary galleries and top-tier restaurants, bordering the lakes and museums of Chapultepec.

dishes.name: Tacos al pastor
dishes.description: Pork marinated in chili and achiote, stacked on a vertical spit, shaved onto small corn tortillas and crowned with pineapple, onion and cilantro.

dishes.name: Chilaquiles
dishes.description: Fried tortilla pieces simmered in red or green salsa and topped with crema, cheese, onion and often a fried egg or shredded chicken: the ultimate breakfast.

dishes.name: Guajolota
dishes.description: A steamed tamal tucked inside a bolillo roll and sold from morning street carts, a gloriously filling carb-on-carb commuter classic.

dishes.name: Chiles en nogada
dishes.description: Poblano chilies stuffed with spiced meat and fruit, draped in walnut cream and scattered with pomegranate seeds, served mainly in August and September.

dishes.name: Pulque
dishes.description: A milky, slightly sour drink fermented from agave sap, sipped since Aztec times and revived in old-school pulquerías, often blended with fruit or oats.

events.name: Vive Latino
events.description: Latin America's biggest rock-in-Spanish festival packs a stadium complex for a weekend of rock, ska, cumbia, hip-hop and indie acts.

events.name: Grito de Independencia
events.description: On the night of September 15, the president rings a bell and cries '¡Viva México!' from the National Palace to a packed Zócalo, followed by fireworks and a military parade the next day.

events.name: Día de Muertos
events.description: Marigold-covered altars fill homes, plazas and cemeteries around November 1–2, and a spectacular parade of giant skeletons and catrinas sweeps through the center in the days before.

events.name: Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe
events.description: Millions of pilgrims, many walking for days, converge on the Basilica of Guadalupe around December 12 for mariachi serenades, dancers and all-night vigils.

attractions.name: Teotihuacan
attractions.description: Two thousand years ago this was one of the largest cities on Earth, and its colossal Pyramids of the Sun and Moon still dominate a valley about an hour northeast of the capital. Walk the broad Avenue of the Dead past temple platforms and faded jaguar murals, and bring sunscreen, a hat and water.
attractions.bookingTip: Arrive for the 9 a.m. opening, before tour buses and midday heat, and take the direct bus from Terminal Norte if you're not on a tour.

attractions.name: National Museum of Anthropology
attractions.description: Mexico's finest museum covers every pre-Hispanic civilization in a modernist building whose courtyard is sheltered by a giant concrete umbrella that pours a curtain of water from its single column. The Mexica hall, home to the 24-ton Sun Stone, is the showstopper, but the Maya and Oaxaca galleries are just as spellbinding.
attractions.bookingTip: Go on a weekday morning, head straight to the Mexica hall at the back, and save the upstairs ethnography rooms for last.

attractions.name: Zócalo
attractions.description: One of the largest public squares in the world, a vast stone expanse with a giant flag at its center and a ceaseless swirl of protests, concerts, feather-crowned Aztec dancers and vendors. Framed by the cathedral, the National Palace and the ruins of the Templo Mayor, it's the natural starting point for any visit.
attractions.bookingTip: Step into the National Palace on the east side to see Diego Rivera's epic murals; entry is free but bring your passport as ID.

attractions.name: Metropolitan Cathedral
attractions.description: Nearly 250 years in the making, the largest cathedral in the Americas blends Renaissance, Baroque and Neoclassical styles across its towering facade. Inside, gilded altarpieces glow in candlelight, and a long pendulum hanging in the nave reveals how the building is slowly sinking into the soft lakebed.
attractions.bookingTip: Pay a few dollars at the side entrance to join a guided bell-tower climb with close-up views over the Zócalo.

attractions.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
attractions.description: A wedding cake of white Italian marble crowned with an orange-and-gold dome, this is Mexico's grandest concert hall and a showcase for its great muralists. Rivera and Siqueiros murals cover the upper walls, while the Ballet Folklórico performs beneath a shimmering glass stage curtain made by Tiffany.
attractions.bookingTip: Book the Ballet Folklórico's Wednesday or Sunday performance ahead, and see the facade lit up at night from a terrace across the street.

attractions.name: Chapultepec Castle
attractions.description: Crowning a wooded hill in the city's great park, this is the only castle in North America ever used by a reigning monarch, once home to Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota. Wander stained-glass galleries and the rooftop garden, then gaze down Paseo de la Reforma, the boulevard Maximilian built to link his palace with the old city.
attractions.bookingTip: The walk up from the park entrance is steep, so allow 15 minutes, and avoid Sundays when residents enter free and lines are long.

attractions.name: Frida Kahlo Museum
attractions.description: Frida Kahlo was born, lived and died in this cobalt-blue house in Coyoacán, still filled with her brushes, corsets, folk-art collection and the garden she adored. Seeing her wheelchair parked before the easel in her studio is quietly unforgettable.
attractions.bookingTip: Tickets are sold online only and weekend slots sell out a week or more ahead; add the small photo permit if you want pictures inside.

attractions.name: Xochimilco
attractions.description: A web of Aztec-era canals on the city's southern edge, where flower-painted trajinera boats drift past chinampa gardens while floating vendors sell grilled corn, micheladas and mariachi serenades. Weekends turn it into one big floating party; weekdays reveal a calmer world of herons and plant nurseries.
attractions.bookingTip: Boats are priced per hour for the whole boat at a posted official rate of roughly 650 pesos, so gather a group and agree on the time before boarding.

attractions.name: Arena México
attractions.description: The cathedral of lucha libre hosts masked high-flyers, villainous rudos and roaring families several nights a week. Grab a beer, learn a few chants from your neighbors and buy a sequined mask from the stalls outside; it's pure, joyful theater.
attractions.bookingTip: Buy tickets at the box office or official site rather than from touts, and leave valuables at the hotel since the surrounding Doctores streets are gritty after dark.

attractions.name: La Merced Market
attractions.description: The city's largest traditional market is a sprawling, chaotic maze of chili pyramids, piñata makers, candied-fruit stalls and fondas steaming with pozole. It's a full-sensory crash course in Mexican ingredients, so come hungry, bring small bills and keep your bag in front of you.
attractions.bookingTip: Visit with a guide or a cooking class the first time, as the market sprawls across several buildings and some surrounding streets are rough.

hotels.name: Casa Ahuehuete Polanco
hotels.description: A limestone-and-glass hideaway facing the treetops of Chapultepec, with a spa offering temazcal steam rituals, a rooftop pool and suites dressed in Oaxacan textiles and volcanic stone. The concierge can arrange private guides for the anthropology museum a short walk away.

hotels.name: Casona del Tezontle
hotels.description: An 18th-century mansion built of blood-red volcanic stone, with rooms set around an arcaded courtyard and a talavera-tiled fountain. From the roof terrace you can watch the cathedral's bell towers glow at dusk.

hotels.name: Estudio Colibrí
hotels.description: A 1920s Art Deco apartment block reimagined by young Mexican designers, with terrazzo floors, cantera-stone bathrooms and furniture from local workshops. The ground-floor mezcal bar and plant-filled patio draw a stylish neighborhood crowd.

hotels.name: Hostal Azotea Nopal
hotels.description: Clean, colorful dorms and a handful of private rooms two blocks from the Zócalo, with a rooftop bar that hosts taco nights and free walking tours every morning. The staff are walking encyclopedias of cheap eats.

hotels.name: Los Coyotes Garden Apartments
hotels.description: Airy apartments around a bougainvillea-draped garden on a cobbled Coyoacán street, each with a full kitchen and hand-painted tiles. Frida's Blue House, the churro stands and the main plaza are all a short stroll away.

hotels.name: Hotel Ahuizotl Condesa
hotels.description: A slim boutique hotel above a tree-lined Condesa boulevard, with jewel-toned rooms, balconies wrapped in jacaranda branches and a rooftop plunge pool. The woods and castle of Chapultepec are a pleasant 15-minute walk.

restaurants.name: Taquería La Piña Voladora
restaurants.description: Taqueros shave marinated pork from a flame-licked spit and flick a sliver of pineapple onto each tortilla with a showman's flourish. It fills with wrestling fans after the matches and keeps serving into the early hours.
restaurants.signatureDish: Tacos al pastor with pineapple, onion and cilantro

restaurants.name: El Comal de las Siete Salsas
restaurants.description: A family-run market stall where blue-corn tlacoyos and huaraches puff up on a clay griddle before being piled with nopales, fresh cheese and your pick of seven salsas. Grab a stool and eat shoulder to shoulder with vendors on their break.
restaurants.signatureDish: Blue-corn tlacoyo with fava beans, nopales and salsa verde

restaurants.name: Café de Olla y Canela
restaurants.description: A cozy café where clay pots of cinnamon-spiced coffee simmer all morning and chilaquiles arrive crunchy under tangy salsa verde. The basket of pan dulce, with conchas still warm from the oven, is dangerous.
restaurants.signatureDish: Chilaquiles verdes with fried egg and café de olla

restaurants.name: Casa Tlecuil
restaurants.description: An open wood-fired hearth anchors this hushed dining room, where a tasting menu travels from Yucatán to Baja using heirloom corn, native herbs and delicacies like huitlacoche and escamoles. Pairings mix natural Mexican wines with rare small-batch mezcals.
restaurants.signatureDish: Duck in Oaxacan black mole with heirloom blue-corn tortillas

restaurants.name: Marisquería Tres Mareas
restaurants.description: A buzzing, sunlit lunch spot where chilangos linger for hours over tostadas, aguachile and whole grilled fish. Share the pescado a la talla, painted half with red chili adobo and half with green herb sauce.
restaurants.signatureDish: Pescado a la talla with red and green adobo

restaurants.name: Cantina El Gallo Desvelado
restaurants.description: Swinging doors, a long mahogany bar and white-jacketed waiters who bring free botanas with every round of drinks. Stay long enough and a guitar trio will offer to serenade your table.

restaurants.name: Café Cedro Libanés
restaurants.description: A tiled dining room honoring the Lebanese families who settled downtown a century ago and gave Mexico the taco árabe, the spit-roasted ancestor of al pastor. Order kibbeh, stuffed grape leaves and tacos árabes wrapped in soft flatbread with smoky chipotle salsa.

restaurants.name: Azotea Cempasúchil
restaurants.description: A rooftop terrace strung with marigold-orange lanterns and framed by the golden dome of Bellas Artes across the Alameda. Come for sunset and stay for tlayudas, mezcal flights and weekend DJ sets.
restaurants.signatureDish: Tlayuda with tasajo, quesillo and black-bean paste

experiences.name: Sunrise Balloon over the Pyramids
experiences.description: Float silently above the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon as dawn washes the valley pink, with your pilot tracing the ancient city's layout below. Land to a sparkling toast and a hearty Mexican breakfast before walking the ruins with a guide.

experiences.name: Xochimilco Trajinera Fiesta
experiences.description: Board a private flower-painted trajinera with a small group, a cooler of cold beer and pulque, and a picnic of tacos de canasta. A mariachi boat pulls alongside for a serenade before you drift into quieter canals to visit a working chinampa farm.

experiences.name: Mole from Scratch Market Class
experiences.description: Shop La Merced with a cook from Oaxaca, choosing dried chilies, seeds and chocolate by smell and taste, then toast, grind and simmer a mole negro in her rooftop kitchen. Lunch is everything you make, with handmade tortillas and agua fresca.

experiences.name: Masks & Mezcal Lucha Night
experiences.description: Pick up your own wrestling mask, learn the chants from a lucha-obsessed guide and cheer from reserved seats as rudos and técnicos fly across the ring. Afterward, toast the winners with a mezcal tasting and late-night tacos al pastor.
